name: Social-engineering scenario analysis
theory_paragraphs: \term{Social engineering} means attacking the \imp{human, not the machine}. Instead of breaking cryptography or exploiting a software bug, the attacker manipulates a person into voluntarily handing over information, money, or access. Why does this work? Because security systems ultimately trust human decisions: if a user can be tricked into typing their password into a fake page, approving a \term{BankID} request (BankID is Sweden's national electronic-ID app: people use it on their phone to log in and to sign or confirm payments and official actions, so a tricked confirmation works like a real signature), or opening a malicious attachment, all the technical protection underneath is bypassed. A useful mental model: the attacker is running an exploit against the human operating system --- against habits like politeness, trust in authority, helpfulness, and panic under pressure. Everyone is susceptible; getting fooled says something about the attacker's skill, not the victim's intelligence. Social engineering is the entry point of a huge share of real incidents (phishing campaigns, ransomware intrusions, identity theft, payment fraud).

A social-engineering attack usually follows recognizable \term{attack phases}: (1) \term{research} --- gather fragments about the target from public sources (hitta.se, hemnet.se, LinkedIn, Facebook); (2) \term{pretexting} --- invent a believable role and scenario and build rapport and trust; (3) \term{get the data} --- exploit the established trust to extract credentials, PII (personally identifiable information: name, address, personnummer, account numbers), money, or a malware install; (4) keep the connection alive without raising suspicion; (5) \term{combine} many small, individually harmless pieces of data into a complete picture (e.g. the last four digits of a \term{personnummer} --- the Swedish personal identity number, consisting of the holder's birthdate (year-month-day) followed by four individual digits, so a birthdate plus the last four digits reveal the whole number --- spoken on the phone, completed with a birthdate found via a public directory); and (6) \term{use} the result. \imp{Small data fragments are valuable because they aggregate.} Never dismiss a leak as 'only four digits'.

The course expects you to name specific \term{manipulation strategies} and pair each with the \term{human trait} it exploits. Learn this table:
\begin{tightitem}
\item \term{Pretext: trappings of the role} --- caller ID showing a real number, hold music, case/order numbers, official logos, lookalike domains, marketing-style language, 'we never send links' disclaimers. Exploits \term{attribution/trust}: we trust whatever looks and sounds like the legitimate role.
\item \term{Threat / fear} --- 'the payment has already come through', 'your account will be emptied'. Exploits \term{reduced cognitive ability}: fear literally degrades systematic, careful thinking.
\item \term{Urgency / rush} --- 'within 24 hours', 'before the deadline tomorrow'. Exploits the same reduced cognition, this time via time pressure: hurrying skips verification steps.
\item \term{Rapport / empathy / light banter} --- small talk, jokes, shared experiences ('moving is so stressful, we also moved this year'). Exploits \term{liking}: people agree to more requests from someone they like.
\item \term{Peer pressure / social proof} --- 'your neighbours the Ericssons and the Smiths already donated'. Exploits the desire to conform and not deviate from social expectations.
\item \term{Altercasting} --- pushing the victim into a role: the \term{victim role} (the attacker creates a problem, e.g. a fake fraudulent order, then 'fixes' it --- exploits \term{reactance} and builds gratitude) or the \term{helper role} ('people are suffering, we need your help' --- exploits the desire to be helpful and cooperative).
\end{tightitem}

Technical aids make the pretext convincing: \term{lookalike domains} (paypa1.com with the digit 1, gmaill.com with double l, junk subdomains like stockholmhelps.paypa1.com where only the \emph{last} part of the hostname is the real domain), spoofed caller ID, QR codes that open BankID confirmations, and attachments delivered only after trust is built. Remember how to read a hostname: the real owner is the registered domain directly before the top-level domain, so stockholmhelps.paypa1.com belongs to paypa1.com, \emph{not} to PayPal. Countermeasures split into \term{organizational} (clear protocols that are actually enforced, awareness training, simple rules for what counts as sensitive, ID required before restricted actions, a culture where saying 'no' is acceptable) and \term{technical} (spam/phishing filters, two-factor authentication (\term{2FA}: a second proof of identity on top of the password, e.g. a BankID confirmation, so a stolen password alone is not enough), least privilege, separation of duty).

How the exam grades this: part (a) is scored as \imp{triples: strategy name + human trait + quoted scenario line}, typically 1 point per element (3 strategies x 3 elements = 9 points). A strategy without its trait or its quote loses most of its points. Part (b), 'what did the attacker get', is graded conservatively: list \imp{only gains the scenario's final state explicitly proves} --- one true gain suffices for the point, but any over-claim (e.g. 'got the password' when only digits were given) loses it. Part (c) wants two concrete, realistic follow-on attacks consistent with the harvest: malware hidden in the opened attachment (ransomware, credential stealer), the confirmed money transfer, account takeover where no 2FA exists, identity theft at services where a personnummer alone suffices as authentication, credential reuse on other sites.
theory_cheatsheet: Strategy--trait pairs: role trappings $\rightarrow$ attribution/trust; fear/threat $\rightarrow$ reduced cognitive ability; urgency/rush $\rightarrow$ no systematic thinking under time pressure; rapport/banter $\rightarrow$ liking; peer pressure $\rightarrow$ desire to conform; altercasting: victim role (attacker creates a problem, then `fixes' it) $\rightarrow$ reactance/gratitude; helper role (`people suffering, we need your help') $\rightarrow$ desire to help.
Attack phases: research, pretext, get data, keep connection, combine data, use it. \imp{Small data fragments aggregate.}
Grading template for part (a): each strategy is a triple (strategy name + human trait + quoted line). One point per element.
Part (b): only what the final state proves; \imp{over-claiming loses the point}.
Part (c) follow-ons: malware in the attachment, money from a confirmed transfer, account takeover without 2FA, identity theft where a personnummer suffices, credential reuse.
Hostname reading: the real owner is the label right before the TLD --- stockholmhelps.paypa1.com is \emph{not} PayPal.
identify_givens: A detailed narrative or transcript of a scam: an attacker (phishing email/SMS, vishing phone call, fake charity/company/bank) contacts a named victim, with quoted attacker lines, victim actions (clicking, calling back, entering credentials, opening attachments, confirming with BankID/PayPal), and the final state of what was revealed or executed. Often mentions public data sources the attacker combined (hitta.se, hemnet.se) and lookalike domains (paypa1.com, gmaill.com).
identify_target: (a) Identify 3 manipulation strategies, name the human trait each exploits, and quote/mention the exact scenario lines supporting each; (b) state concretely what the attacker obtained; (c) give two examples of what the attacker can do now (follow-on attacks).
identify_keywords: quote or mention the parts of the scenario
what can the attacker do now
strategy_name: Strategy-trait-quote triangulation, then concrete harvest and follow-on attacks

algorithm.action: Map each move to a named strategy
algorithm.detail: Label each move with the course's strategy vocabulary: \term{pretext} (trappings of the role), \term{altercasting} (putting the victim into a victim or helper role, e.g. create-then-fix a problem), \term{urgency/rush}, \term{threat/fear}, \term{peer pressure/social proof}, \term{rapport/empathy/light banter}.

For each strategy-trait pair, quote or precisely reference the supporting scenario line (e.g. 'the payment has already come through' for fear). \imp{Deliver full triples: strategy, trait, quote.} The rubric typically awards one point per element, so a strategy without its trait or quote forfeits most of its points.

Enumerate only what the transcript's final state proves the attacker obtained: opened/executed attachment, credentials entered on the lookalike site, full personnummer or other PII, a confirmed BankID/PayPal transfer, phone number. Do not list anything not evidenced in the story --- \imp{one true gain suffices, but any incorrect claim loses the point}.

Provide two realistic next steps consistent with the harvest: hidden malware in the attachment (ransomware, credential stealer) even if payment is refused; money if a transfer was confirmed; initiating further transactions the victim is groomed to confirm; account takeover where no 2FA exists; identity theft at services where a personnummer alone suffices as authentication; credential reuse on other sites.

variations.name: Callback phishing (vishing) instead of an inbound link
variations.detail: The initial email carries no link or attachment; the victim is lured into calling the attacker's number and the attack happens live by phone, with any attachment arriving in a later 'form' mail. Treat hold music, 'we never include links' disclaimers and marketing style as role trappings, and note the extra harvest channel: spoken partial personnummer completed via a public directory lookup. Trap: do not claim the first email itself carried malware.

variations.name: Charity/donation scam with social proof
variations.detail: The lever is peer pressure ('the neighbours have already donated') plus an urgency deadline and a helper-role pretext ('people are suffering'). Name social proof and altercasting instead of fear; the harvest is payment credentials via a lookalike redirect (letter swapped for a digit). Trap: explicitly notice the domain substitution as part of the pretext.

variations.name: Grading granularity of part (a)
variations.detail: Typical rubric: 3 strategies x (strategy + trait + quote), one point each. Strategies without trait or quote forfeit two-thirds of the points; more than three triples is fine since sample answers list 4--5 acceptable options. Always write full triples.

variations.name: What-counts-as-harvest trap in part (b)
variations.detail: Official solutions mark part (b) correct if at least one true gain is mentioned and no incorrect ones --- over-claiming ('got the money' before the BankID confirmation, 'got the password' when only digits were given) loses the point. List only gains explicitly shown in the scenario's final state.

walkthrough_problem: Social engineering --- Safe Account: Sara, who lives in Lund, receives an SMS from `PostNord': `Your parcel is held at customs. Pay the SEK 45 fee within 24 hours or it will be returned to the sender.' The link leads to postn0rd.se, a pixel-perfect copy of the real PostNord site, where Sara enters her debit-card number, expiry date and CVV (the three-digit security code printed on the back of the card, used to prove the buyer physically holds the card). Two days later her phone rings; the display shows her bank's official support number. `Mikael from the fraud department' greets her warmly, asks how the weather is in Lund, and jokes about the rain he biked through that morning. He then says several customers in her area were hit this week, that case number FB-22114 has been opened, and that two suspicious transactions totalling SEK 14 500 are pending on her account: `if we do not act within the hour, the account will be emptied.' He asks Sara to state her full personnummer `so I can be sure it is really you', then instructs her to move her savings to a `shielded safe account' the bank has created for her, adding the new account as a payee in her banking app. Sara confirms the SEK 12 000 transfer by scanning the QR code with BankID, and Mikael thanks her: `you have been most helpful --- together we caught the thief.' (a) Identify 3 strategies used by the social engineer; for each, name the human trait exploited and quote the parts of the scenario you refer to. (b) What did the attacker get? (c) Give two examples of what the attacker can do now.

walkthrough_steps.work: Inventory every manipulation move before naming anything: fake PostNord SMS with a 24-hour deadline; lookalike domain postn0rd.se (digit `0' for letter `o'); spoofed bank caller ID plus a case number (FB-22114) and a `fraud department' title; small talk about Lund's weather and biking through rain; `several customers in your area were hit'; fear hook (SEK 14 500 pending, `account emptied within the hour'); a created crisis that Mikael then `fixes'; closing flattery (`together we caught the thief'). \emph{Beginner note:} write this inventory on the exam paper first --- it guarantees you will not run out of triples and prevents quoting the same line twice for two different strategies.

Map the moves to named strategies (any three of): 1) pretext: trappings of the role; 2) threat/fear; 3) urgency/rush; 4) rapport/light banter; 5) altercasting into the \term{victim role} --- Mikael creates a problem (the fake fraud crisis) and then `fixes' it with the `safe account', which is exactly the create-and-fix pattern. \emph{Beginner note 1:} use the course's exact vocabulary (`trappings of the role', `altercasting'), not paraphrases like `he pretended to be the bank' --- the grader matches against the named strategies. \emph{Beginner note 2:} keep the two altercasting roles separate, exactly as the official rubric does: create-and-fix is the \emph{victim} role and exploits \emph{reactance}; the \emph{helper} role is a different move (`people are suffering, we need your help') exploiting the desire to help, and it is not the mechanism here.

Attach the human trait to each chosen strategy: role trappings exploit attribution/trust (we trust what looks and sounds like the real institution); fear and urgency exploit reduced cognitive ability under stress and time pressure (panic and hurry shut down careful verification); rapport exploits liking (people agree to more from someone they like); the victim-role altercasting exploits \term{reactance} plus gratitude --- Sara reacts against the threat of losing her money, and when Mikael `saves' her she feels grateful and complies. \emph{Beginner note:} the trait must be a \emph{mechanism} (`fear reduces systematic thinking'), not a restatement (`she was scared').

Quote the evidence to complete the triples: role trappings --- `the display shows her bank's official support number', `case number FB-22114', `pixel-perfect copy ... postn0rd.se'; fear/urgency --- `pay within 24 hours or it will be returned', `several customers in your area were hit this week', `two suspicious transactions totalling SEK 14 500', `if we do not act within the hour, the account will be emptied'; rapport --- `asks how the weather is in Lund, and jokes about the rain he biked through'; victim role --- the created crisis (fake pending transactions) that Mikael then `fixes' via the `shielded safe account', sealed by the closing flattery `together we caught the thief'. Any three full triples earn full marks. \emph{Mistake to avoid 1:} a strategy name alone is worth only 1 of 3 points; the rubric pays per element. \emph{Mistake to avoid 2:} do not label `several customers in your area were hit' as peer pressure/social proof --- Sara is not asked to imitate anyone's behaviour; the line establishes that the fraud wave is real, so it is evidence for fear/threat (or role trappings), not conformity.

(b) The attacker got: Sara's full debit-card details (number, expiry, CVV) entered on postn0rd.se; her full personnummer stated on the phone; and a BankID-confirmed SEK 12 000 transfer to the attacker's `safe account'. \emph{Mistake to avoid:} do not add the SEK 45 fee --- the scenario shows Sara entering her card details but never states the fee payment completed --- and do not add `her banking password' or `her BankID', which the scenario never shows either. The official grading rule is: at least one true gain and no incorrect ones; a single over-claim forfeits the point.

(c) Follow-on attacks (any two): use or sell the card details for \term{card-not-present fraud} (online or phone purchases where the merchant never sees the physical card, so the card number, expiry date and CVV alone are enough to pay); keep calling with new `safe account' emergencies while the grooming holds, since Sara has proven she will confirm BankID requests; commit identity theft --- take loans or order goods at services where a personnummer plus card data suffices as authentication; target Sara again (or her contacts) as a proven compliant victim, e.g. with a `refund' lure carrying malware. \emph{Beginner note:} each follow-on must be \emph{consistent with the harvest} --- do not propose attacks that need data the attacker never obtained.

exam_questions.problem: Eric gets an email from orders <no-reply@northernfitness.se> confirming a `Well-Fit Supreme Unlimited Membership' (Order \#491625, Account \#366481, SEK 9999 via Klarna), written in polished marketing style, giving a customer-service phone number, and stating `We will never include links or attachments in our e-mails to you.' Eric has not ordered this and calls the number. He is put on hold to music (Eye of the Tiger). `Arnold' answers, suggests friends or family may have signed him up (`people get a bit pushy about fitness towards the New Year, I hope they don't also push a diet on you like my colleagues and their constant talk about carbs'), and asks for Eric's name and the last four digits of his personnummer `just to confirm that it's really you'. Eric gives the digits; Arnold looks up Eric's phone number on hitta.se and gets his birthdate to complete the personnummer. Arnold then confirms the membership and says `the payment has come through from your Klarna account already, well done!' Eric asks to cancel; Arnold says he has the right to cancel within 2 weeks and will email a cancellation form, after which a BankID request will confirm the reimbursement. Eric opens the mail and the attachment, fills out the form, clicks confirm, scans the QR code with BankID and confirms the request `Northern Fitness Reimbursement --- SEK 9999'. (a) [9 p] Identify 3 strategies used by the social engineer; for each, identify the human trait they exploit and quote or mention the parts of the scenario you refer to. (b) [1 p] What did the attacker get? (c) [2 p] Give two examples of what the attacker can do now.

solution_steps.work: List the manipulation moves: a fake order confirmation for something never ordered (a created problem); a polished marketing-style email with order/account numbers; the disclaimer `we will never include links or attachments'; a published `customer service' number that Eric himself calls (callback phishing); on-hold music (Eye of the Tiger); friendly banter about pushy fitness friends and colleagues talking about carbs; a request for `only' the last four personnummer digits; the claim that SEK 9999 has already been paid from his Klarna account; and a `cancellation' that actually sends Eric an attachment plus a BankID confirmation.

Official sample answers (any three): 1) \term{pretext: trappings of the role}; 2) \term{threat/fear}; 3) \term{building rapport / showing empathy / light banter}; 4) \term{pretext: put into victim role} (altercasting --- the attacker creates the fake order and then `fixes' it via the cancellation).

Traits per the sample solution: role trappings exploit \term{attribution/trust}; threat/fear exploits \term{reduced cognitive ability}; rapport exploits liking --- `people agree to more from someone they like'; the victim-role pretext exploits \term{reactance} (altercasting).

Quotes per the sample solution: role trappings --- the plausible story, the statement that they never include links or attachments, the marketing style of the email, the on-hold music; fear --- `the payment of SEK 9999 has already come through'; rapport --- talking about people pushing fitness or diets; victim role --- creating the fake order and then pretending to fix the problem. Each full triple (strategy + trait + quote) is worth 3 points.

Sample solution: the attacker got Eric to open a file attached to an email, got him to confirm a money transfer with BankID, got the full personnummer (four digits spoken + birthdate looked up on hitta.se), and the phone number. Grading note: counted correct if at least one listed gain is mentioned and \emph{no incorrect ones}.

Sample solution: the attachment can have hidden malware, e.g. ransomware or a credential stealer, even if Eric does not authorize the bank transfer; if he did authorize it, the attacker gets the money; and the attacker can mount identity-theft attacks in places that do not verify a personnummer with any other factor of authentication.

exam_questions.answer: (a) e.g. role-trappings/trust (hold music, `we never include links', marketing style), fear/reduced cognition (`payment has already come through'), rapport/liking (fitness and diet banter), or victim-role altercasting (create-then-fix the fake order); (b) an opened attachment, a BankID-confirmed SEK 9999 transfer, the full personnummer, and the phone number; (c) hidden malware (ransomware/credential theft), keep the money, identity theft where a personnummer alone suffices.

exam_questions.problem: Emil, a social-engineering attacker, combines data from hemnet.se (recently sold apartments) and hitta.se (new residents and neighbours) and calls Victoria. `Hej! Am I speaking with Victoria? This is Emil Karlsson. I'm with the organization Stockholm Helps. We work with Stockholms Stad and individual housing associations. We've worked with yours, Igelkotten13, so you probably remember how it works?' Victoria says she just moved in. Emil replies: `Oh, I'll briefly explain, but I will not take much of your time, I know there is so much to do when you move, such a hassle! We also moved earlier this year, that was stressful, we still haven't unpacked all the boxes! Anyhow, in short, now at the start of winter and with the current conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine, many people are displaced and suffering and we need an extra push in donations. And this year, Stockholms Stad has pledged to match any donations given before Lucia, tomorrow. So we're busy calling around for a final push. Every krona counts! Several people in your building have already donated, I see here, on your floor the Ericssons and the Smiths, for example. How much would you be willing to contribute?' After some back and forth, Emil texts Victoria a link to the donation site with buttons for amounts and payment methods. Victoria clicks 200 SEK, chooses PayPal, is redirected to stockholmhelps.paypa1.com and fills in her login information. She gets a popup with a receipt to download, and downloads the file. (a) [9 p] Identify 3 strategies used by the social engineer; for each, identify the human trait they exploit and quote or mention the parts of the scenario you refer to. (b) [1 p] What did the attacker get? (c) [2 p] Give two examples of what the attacker can do now.

solution_steps.work: List the manipulation moves: pre-research combining hemnet.se and hitta.se (knows her name, building, floor, neighbours' names); a charity pretext (`Stockholm Helps') claiming cooperation with Stockholms Stad and her own housing association Igelkotten13; empathy banter about the stress of moving (`we also moved earlier this year, still haven't unpacked'); a suffering-people appeal (conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine); a deadline (`before Lucia, tomorrow', `final push'); named neighbours who `already donated'; and a payment redirect to the lookalike domain stockholmhelps.paypa1.com ending in a file download.

Official sample answers (any three): 1) \term{rush/urgency}; 2) \term{peer pressure}; 3) \term{building rapport / showing empathy}; 4) \term{pretext: trappings of the role}; 5) \term{pretext: put into helper role}.

Traits per the sample solution: urgency exploits \term{reduced cognitive ability} under time pressure; peer pressure exploits that `people want to be helpful, cooperate, be nice, not deviate from social expectations'; rapport exploits liking --- `people agree to more from someone they like'; role trappings exploit \term{attribution/trust}; the helper role exploits the \term{desire to help}.

Quotes per the sample solution: urgency --- `before tomorrow' (the Lucia matching deadline); peer pressure --- `several people in your building have already donated ... the Ericssons and the Smiths'; rapport --- `moving is stressful, also moved this year'; role trappings --- the plausible story, having worked with the named housing association and Stockholms Stad; helper role --- `people suffering'. Each full triple (strategy + trait + quote) is worth 3 points.

Sample solution: the attacker got Victoria's PayPal login credentials (entered on the lookalike stockholmhelps.paypa1.com) and got her to download a file. \emph{Trap:} the 200 SEK was never shown to be paid --- do not claim the attacker got the donation money yet; only credentials and the download are proven.

Sample solution: the attacker can now get the donation by initiating a real PayPal transaction and having Victoria confirm it; if no two-factor authentication is set up, use her PayPal account for other transactions or even change her credentials (full account takeover); and the downloaded file could be malware, e.g. ransomware.

exam_questions.answer: (a) e.g. urgency/reduced cognition (`before Lucia, tomorrow'), peer pressure/conformity (`the Ericssons and the Smiths already donated'), rapport/liking (moving-is-stressful banter), role-trappings/trust (Stockholms Stad, Igelkotten13), helper-role/desire to help (`people suffering'); (b) Victoria's PayPal login credentials and a downloaded file; (c) initiate a real PayPal transaction for her to confirm, take over the account if no 2FA, malware such as ransomware in the file.
